verdicts.trueWording: “in part because they find AI poems more straightforward”
verdicts.note: Discussion, raw page: “We propose that people rate AI poems more highly across all metrics in part because they find AI poems more straightforward.” Quote verbatim; every limb supported. Only softening dropped by the claim is the authors' “in part” (they offer it as a partial, not sole, explanation).

Discussion, raw page: “In each of the 5 AI-generated poems used in the assessment study (Study 2), the subject of the poem is fairly obvious… These poems rarely use complex metaphors.” Quote verbatim; the referent of “These poems” is exactly the assessment-study AI poems, so the claim's scoping limb holds.

verdicts.trueWording: “(144 explanations vs. 29 explanations)” for human vs AI
verdicts.note: Discussion, raw page: “participants use variations of the phrase ‘doesn’t make sense’ for human-authored poems more often than they do for AI-generated poems when explaining their discrimination responses (144 explanations vs. 29 explanations).” Quote verbatim, both figures and both directions correct. Pedantic note: the page counts 144/29 explanations containing the phrase, not 144/29 utterances of it; the counts come from the discrimination study (Study 1).

verdicts.trueWording: “experience with poetry did not improve discrimination performance”
verdicts.note: Results, “The effect of experience with poetry” exploratory model. Quote verbatim, and independently corroborated: “none of the effects measuring poetry experience had a significant positive effect on accuracy” (McFadden's R2 = 0.012). The page's trailing carve-out — “unless that experience allowed them to recognize the specific poems used in the study” — concerns prior exposure to the specific poems (OR = 1.062), not poetry experience, so it does not unseat any limb of the claim.

verdicts.trueWording: “Using ChatGPT 3.5, we generated 5 poems ‘in the style of’ each poet”
verdicts.note: Methods/stimuli. Quote verbatim. Ten-poet limb confirmed on the same page: “We chose 10 English-language poets: Geoffrey Chaucer, William Shakespeare, Samuel Butler, Lord Byron, Walt Whitman, Emily Dickinson, T.S. Eliot, Allen Ginsberg, Sylvia Plath, and Dorothea Lasky”, and “We then generated a total of 50 poems using ChatGPT 3.5” (5 x 10).

verdicts.trueWording: “human out of the loop… we used the first 5 poems generated”
verdicts.note: Methods/stimuli, raw page: “We used a ‘human out of the loop’ paradigm: we used the first 5 poems generated, and did not select the ‘best’ out of a group of poems or provide any feedback or instructions to the model beyond ‘Write a short poem in the style of <poet>’.” Quote verbatim; paradigm, no-selection and no-feedback limbs all explicit.

verdicts.trueWording: “experts preferred human writing in 82.7% of cases under the in-context prompting condition”
verdicts.note: Abstract of arXiv:2601.18353v1 (Chakrabarty & Dhillon, submitted 26 Jan 2026). Quote verbatim. “Pairwise” limb: “Based on blind pairwise comparisons by 28 expert judges and 131 lay judges”; MFA limb: “28 MFA writers (experts)”, and §3.1.1/intro confirm the same 28 writers served as the expert judges. §4.1 localises the 82.7% to the Writing Quality axis (Stylistic Fidelity was 72.0%); the claim, like the abstract, does not name the axis.

verdicts.trueWording: “reversed to 62% preference for AI after fine-tuning on authors’ complete works”
verdicts.note: Abstract; quote verbatim. GPT-4o limb supported in §3.1.3: “The only frontier model… that allows fine-tuning via API is ChatGPT (GPT-4o), so we used that” and “we fine-tune GPT-4o (Version: gpt-4o-2024-08-06)”, on “an author’s entire oeuvre”. §4.1/Figure 7 give the precise figure as 62.2% (Writing Quality). Scope detail: fine-tuning covered 30 of the 50 authors (living authors only).

verdicts.trueWording: “Lay judges, however, consistently preferred AI writing”
verdicts.note: Abstract; quote verbatim, whole claim supported. §4.1 nuances rather than contradicts it: under in-context prompting lay judges showed “weaker or no clear preference” (44.0% / 52.7% human), and after fine-tuning clearly preferred AI (68.9% / 80.0%).

verdicts.trueWording: “possibly because fine-tuning eliminates the stylistic tics… experts used to distinguish”
verdicts.note: §4.1; quote verbatim, including the em-dashed list “clíchés, awkward phrasing, overly ornamental language” and the trailing “that experts used to distinguish human from AI-generated text”. The one softening the claim drops is modal: the authors hedge the mechanism as “possibly because”, so “attribute” states with more confidence than the page does — it remains the only explanation the page offers for the expert shift.

verdicts.trueWording: “both experts (81.1%) and lay evaluators (80.0%) strongly preferred AI-generated writing”
verdicts.note: Figure 7 caption, Stylistic Fidelity, Fine-tuned condition; quote verbatim and both figures correct (the caption's alt text gives the complements, 18.9% and 20.0% human). Unit detail: the caption calls these “the proportion of evaluators preferring”, while §4.1 says the fine-tuned data are N=90 majority-vote pairwise comparisons per group — the claim mirrors the caption's own wording.

§4.2 opening sentence, raw page: “Lay judges disproportionately reward writing based on whether it ‘flows well’, is ‘more organized,’ or whether ‘easier to follow.’” Quote verbatim and all three justifications named in order; the page adds that these rationales accompanied their stated preferences.

verdicts.trueWording: “fine-tuning requires 583 times more number of tokens on average”
verdicts.note: §3.1.3, raw page: “Figures 5, 6 show that fine-tuning requires 583 times more number of tokens on average compared to In-context Prompting”, repeated in the Figure 6 caption. Quote verbatim; comparator (in-context prompting) and “on average” both explicit.

verdicts.trueWording: “OpenAI’s GPT-4o, Anthropic’s Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Google’s Gemini 1.5 Pro”
verdicts.note: §3.1.3, In-context Prompting: “We converted the identical writing prompt provided to writers into long-context prompts for three widely used large language models: OpenAI’s GPT-4o, Anthropic’s Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Google’s Gemini 1.5 Pro.” Quote verbatim (curly apostrophes match); “three models” and “under in-context prompting” both explicit — one excerpt per author per LLM, 150 total.

verdicts.trueWording: “plot, character development, or structure might not be accurately reflected”
verdicts.note: §3.1.4, raw page: “Our study examines shorter (up to 450-word) excerpts and because of this, broader creative elements such as plot, character development, or structure might not be accurately reflected.” Quote verbatim and the concession limb explicit. Two shadings: the writing brief was a 200–450 word excerpt (the claim gives only the ceiling), and the page's hedge is “might not be accurately reflected” rather than flatly “unmeasured”.
